doc.title: Dave Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, Connecticut, November 21, 2001

title: Brodsky Quartet and 'Ode to Joy' in 5/4
summary: Brubeck explains how he reluctantly accepted the Brodsky Quartet's request and found Beethoven's 'Ode to Joy' works in 5/4.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Very interesting. The piece you’re working on now, or the pieces, is it choral in nature or orchestral?
One of the last things I wrote was, do you know the Brodsky String Quartet?
They just recorded my “String Quartet” have you got that?

Well they asked me to do a piece that they’re doing — the last time they did a piece like this they made about a million two hundred thousand for the poor, and they gave, through the BBC they gave all the money. And they do kind of far out things. So they’re doing Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy” and they’re asking all kinds of composers to contribute their version of “Ode to Joy.” You know who Tom Waits is?
Well he’s done it for drain pipe.
He’s done it to be played on a drain pipe?

On the drain pipe. And so various composers are doing this thing. So they asked me to do it and I thought oh that’s sacrilege. The “Ode to Joy?” And so you know I don’t always accept things. I said oh I don’t want to do that. And I think about it, because it won’t leave my mind, and I thought why it’s perfect in 5/4 time. [scats] one-two — three-four- five. One-two-three-four-five, One-two-three-four-five. And then the second theme [scats]. So they’re not waiting for the broadcast, they’re using it for an encore now. They said it works so well.
Isn’t that so interesting that your first reaction is, “oh please.” But I can just see the way you must work, it’s like it gets in there and something starts stirring around.
